Our central, theoryguided expectation was that outgroup germ aversion would emerge as a more consistent predictor of intergroup attitudes than ingroup germ aversion, general germ aversion, infectability concern, or COVID-19 concern. This expectation follows from the idea that pathogen avoidance may become especially relevant to prejudice when the perceived source of infection is socially distant, unfamiliar, or outgroup-based (Bressan, 2021; Bressan, 2023a Bressan, , 2023b;; Faulkner et al., 2004; Fincher et al., 2008; Ji et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2022; Krings et al., 2012; Tybur et al., 2020; Van Leeuwen et al., 2023; cf. Fan et al., 2022; Fan et al., 2024; Van Leeuwen & Petersen, 2018; Van Leeuwen et al., 2025). Accordingly, we examined whether higher outgroup germ aversion predicted stronger ingroup preference and greater outgroup derogation across explicit and implicit outcomes, even after controlling for established diseaseavoidance measures and relevant demographic characteristics.

To create a clearer link between our prediction and analysis, directional expectations below are reported as retrospectively specified, theory-guided tests rather than preregistered confirmatory hypotheses.

H1a-H1d predict that higher Outgroup GA is associated with higher American explicit health ratings (H1a), higher American implicit health scores (H1b), greater warmth towards Americans (H1c), and greater warmth towards White people (H1d). White people are the largest racial category in the sample, not the ingroup of every participant. The covariate strategy was organised around distinct inferential roles. First, ingroup germ aversion, general germ aversion, infectability concern, and COVID-19 concern were included to test whether target-specific germ aversion added information beyond established disease-avoidance constructs. Second, political ideology and individualism were added in a separate block because they are plausible shared correlates of both pathogen avoidance and intergroup attitudes and because COVID-19 was strongly politicised in the United States (Brandt et al., 2025; Fiagbenu, 2025; Ko et al., 2025; O'Shea et al., 2022; Stern & Axt, 2022). The design cannot determine whether they are pre-exposure confounders, consequences, or indicators of broader orientations. Third, age, gender, socioeconomic status, education, religiosity, and race/ethnicity indicators were added as a conservative robustness block because these characteristics may relate to disease avoidance, group attitudes, or study selection. Reporting the stages separately makes clear how the focal associations change before and after each adjustment.

Method

Participants and Sampling

Data were collected through the Project Implicit research website (https://implicit.harvard.edu/implicit/) between March 28 and May 15, 2020, during the first peak of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States and Italy. Participants were volunteers who selected a COVID-19 featured task from the Project Implicit website. The study description stated that participants would need to recognise images of landmarks from the United States, China, Italy, and the United Kingdom, because the task assessed associations between COVID-19-related concepts and people or places from these countries. Participants received no financial compensation, but they were given feedback on their implicit associations at the end of the study.

A total of 5,434 participants provided informed consent. We excluded 343 participants who reported being younger than 18 years old and 38 outliers (above 3 SD; see SM for details). Of the remaining 5,053 participants, 2,417 did not report their country of residence (incomplete data are not uncommon with Project Implicit online volunteers; see O'Shea & Ueda, 2021; Werntz et al., 2023), and 667 resided outside the United States.

Following recommended scoring procedures for the Brief Implicit Association Test (BIAT;

Nosek et al., 2014), participants were also excluded from BIAT analyses if they had error rates above 30%, more than 10% of trials faster than 300 ms, or more than 10% of trials slower than 10,000 ms. Because U.S. residents made up the large majority of respondents, and because the non-U.S. samples were too small for reliable country-specific analyses after random assignment to BIAT conditions, the primary analyses were restricted to U.S. residents. After exclusions, 1,969 participants resided in the United States, compared with 125 in the United Kingdom, 26 in China, and 14 in Italy. A power analysis conducted in G*Power (Faul et al., 2009) indicated that 185 participants would be required to detect an effect of f² = .10 with .80 power given the number of predictors in the regression models. The U.S. sample therefore provided adequate power for the explicit-attitude analyses and for most BIAT analyses, whereas the non-U.S. samples did not.

Available sample sizes varied across analyses because not all participants completed all measures and because participants were randomly assigned to one of three country-specific BIAT conditions. For explicit attitude outcomes, analytic samples ranged from 1,450 to 1,460 participants. For implicit attitude outcomes, samples ranged from 378 to 1,311 participants. The mean age of the U.S. sample was 30.58 years (SD = 13.67), and approximately 84% of participants had completed at least some college education. Most participants reported their gender identity as female (n = 1,283), followed by male (n = 650); 36 participants reported another gender identity or did not provide gender information and were not included in gender-comparative analyses because of the small cell size. Approximately 65% of the final U.S. sample identified as White non-Hispanic, 12% as Asian, 8% as Black, 12% as Hispanic, and 14% as another or mixed racial/ethnic group (1% did not report their race). SM Table J1 reports demographic characteristics and descriptive statistics for the 1,463 participants with complete data on all predictors. Ingroup GA (O'Shea et al., 2022): Four items were adapted from the germ aversion (GA) subscale of the PVD Scale (Duncan et al., 2009) to assess avoidance of pathogens associated with people and environments in participants' local region (e.g., I am comfortable eating street food in my local region [reverse scored]; I often use hand sanitiser in my local region). Responses were made on the same 7-point Likert scale as the original PVD. Higher scores indicated greater ingroup germ aversion. Internal consistency was modest (Cronbach's α = .47; McDonald's ω = .49; mean inter-item correlation = .17), consistent with the use of a brief scale comprising heterogeneous behavioural scenarios rather than interchangeable indicators of a single behaviour (Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994; Streiner, 2003).

Materials

Outgroup GA (O'Shea et al., 2022):

Four parallel items assessed avoidance of pathogens associated with developing/foreign countries using the same behavioural scenarios (e.g., I am comfortable sharing a water bottle with a stranger from a developing country [reverse scored]; I would try to avoid using public toilets in developing countries because of the risk that I may catch something from the previous user). Responses were recorded using the same 7-point Likert scale. Higher scores indicated greater outgroup germ aversion. Internal consistency was modest (Cronbach's α = .55; McDonald's ω = .56; mean inter-item correlation = .24). Because the adapted Ingroup and Outgroup GA scales showed modest internal consistency, we report additional psychometric analyses in the SM.

The Cultural Cognition Worldview Scales (CCW; Kahan, 2012):

The CCWS (α = .70) measures individualism versus collectivism. Participants responded on a 6-point Likert scale (1= "Strongly agree",6= "Strongly disagree") (e.g. Too many people today expect society to do things for them that they should be doing for themselves). Higher scores indicate greater individualism.

Demographics

Participants answered basic demographic questions relating to sex assigned at birth, gender identity (binary-coded; Female= 0; Male= 1), age reported in years, race (White non-Hispanic served as the reference category, with Black, Asian, and Other non-Hispanic categories dummy coded), ethnicity (identity as Hispanic or not), country of primary citizenship, country of residence, education (dichotomised as some college or above = 1, less than some college = 0), and socio-economic status (SES). SES was measured using Adler et al.'s (2000) self-rated ladder scale, which assesses perceived social standing relative to others based on income, education, and occupational attainment, with scores ranging from 1 (low) to 10 (high). Political identity was measured using a 7-point Likert scale (1=Strongly Liberal,7=Strongly Conservative), and both religiosity and personal concern about COVID-19 were each measured on a 1 (Not at All) to 4 (Very Religious/Concerned) Likert Scale.

Explicit Outcome Variables: The Explicit Health/Infectiousness items asked: "To

what extent do you associate [American/Chinese/Italians/Britons (British)] People with

Infected or Healthy?" using a 9-point response scale (1= "Extremely strong association with

Infected",9= "Extremely strong association with Healthy"). The feeling thermometer items asked: "How warm or cold do you feel towards [American/Chinese/Italian/Britons (British)/White/Asian/Black/Brown] People?" with an 11-point scale (0= "Extremely cold/negative" to10= "Extremely warm/positive").

Implicit Outcome Variables: The Brief Implicit Association Test (BIAT):

The BIAT is an adaptation of the IAT (see Sriram & Greenwald, 2009). However, unlike the standard IAT (Greenwald et al., 1998; Greenwald et al., 2022), the BIAT displays only two rather than four category targets on screen in each block and has fewer trials, making it suitable for online administration under time constraints. This design makes the BIAT particularly apt for Decomposing D-score (DD-score) analysis (O'Shea, Glenn, et al., 2020; adapted from Greenwald et al.'s (2003) D-scores), and therefore, the DD-Score can be used to gauge absolute automatic biases/implicit attitudes (one category) rather than relatively (D-score = two categories; see O'Shea & Wiers, 2020). The socially sensitive nature of attributing infection risk to national and racial groups makes the BIAT especially useful in the present context because participants may be reluctant to explicitly report negative attitudes toward outgroups due to impression-management or social-desirability concerns (Greenwald et al., 2009; Kurdi et al., 2019). Implicit measures can therefore provide complementary information that may not be captured fully by self-report measures.

In our BIATs, first participants completed two practice blocks with 12 trials in each, where participants had to sort stimuli (words related to each of the two categories that were: 'Infected, Coronavirus, Germs, Fever, Cough' for 'Infected,' and 'Clean, Hygienic, Sterile, Sanitary' for 'Healthy') that appeared in the middle of the screen (focally) into one of two superordinate attribute categories (Healthy or Infected) that appeared at the top centre of the screen (counterbalanced). Respondents were told to categorise the stimulus as fast and as accurately as they could. If the stimulus matched the superordinate category, an "I" keyboard press must be made, "if item belongs", while an "E" keypress was made, "for all else". After the practice blocks, the target category "Americans", was displayed just below the attribute category and remained fixed for two critical blocks of 44 trials each. The "Healthy" and "Infected" attribute categories followed the same order from the practice blocks. The stimuli representing the "Americans" category included "American People", "American Children", and "American Grandparents", along with the US national flag and two iconic landmarks. An "E" keypress was used for comparable stimuli related to Chinese, Italian and British. Words relating to the category were in green, and words relating to the respective country were in blue (see SM for an example BIAT screenshot). The inter-trial interval (ITI) duration was 250ms.

If they made a mistake, a red "X" appeared until the correct key was pressed, forcing participants to correct an error before a reaction time response was recorded.

After participants completed the "Americans" BIAT, they were randomly assigned to complete an "Italian", "Chinese", or "British" BIAT, where "I" keypresses were used for these focal categories and "E" keypresses were used for the remaining country stimuli.

Each block had an equal number of right and left correct keypresses throughout. Participants were blind to the condition administered. For implicit measures like the BIAT, it is proposed that a task will be easier (and therefore completed faster) when sorting is consistent with one's mental association between stimuli and superordinate category labels (Sriram & Greenwald, 2009). Therefore, we were able to create DD-scores (O'Shea & Wiers, 2020, O'Shea, Glenn, et al., 2020), for each participant towards "Americans" by calculating the average reaction time of sorting "American" and "Healthy" stimuli and subtracting the average reaction time of sorting "American" and "Infected" stimuli together and then dividing the difference score of these mean latencies across the two critical BIAT blocks by the standard deviation of the latencies. A similar DD-score was calculated for the other country (China, Italy, or the UK) to which participants were randomly assigned. A relative score was also generated by subtracting each participant's American DD-score from the other country's DD-score they completed.

Throughout, higher scores on the BIAT indicated greater health rather than infection implicit attitudes towards the target country.

Design/Procedure

The study had a cross-sectional design. Participants first read an information sheet and then gave informed consent. Following demographic questions, participants completed three task blocks in random order: (a) the explicit health/infectiousness and feeling thermometer items (all items randomised), (b) the questionnaire scales, and (c) the BIAT block. The questionnaire block included the randomly ordered Cultural Cognition Worldview Scale and Perceived Vulnerability to Disease (PVD) scale, comprising the infectability concern and general germ-aversion subscales, followed by the adapted Ingroup and Outgroup GA items.

Within the BIAT block, participants completed the U.S. BIAT first and were randomly allocated to complete the China, U.K. or Italy BIAT. The whole task took approximately 15 minutes. Upon completing the BIAT, participants received their U.S. BIAT absolute (DDscore) results and a general debriefing.

Data Analysis Plan

Data were analysed using SPSS version 28 for the primary regression analyses and R version 4.2.2 (R Core Team, 2022), including lavaan version 0.6-21 (Rosseel, 2012), for supplementary analyses and reproducibility checks. Full correlation matrices are provided in the Supplementary Materials (SM). The main text focuses on key correlations, including the correspondence between implicit and explicit health/infectiousness scores (Irving & Smith, 2020).

To evaluate the discriminant validity of the four disease-avoidance measures (infectability concern, general germ aversion [GA], Ingroup GA, and Outgroup GA), we conducted confirmatory factor analyses (CFAs). First, we compared one-and two-factor models of the eight matched Ingroup and Outgroup GA items, with and without residual correlations between identical behavioural scenarios. Second, we compared alternative factor structures across all 23 disease-avoidance items. The explicit outcome ratings were single-item measures, and the BIAT outcomes were computed task scores; they were therefore not included as separate item-level latent factors. Models were estimated using maximum likelihood with robust standard errors and a scaled test statistic (MLR). Model fit, parameter admissibility, and latent factor correlations were examined, with full results reported in SM Appendix Z.

Additional psychometric analyses, including reliability estimates, principal component analyses, item diagnostics, and item response theory analyses, are also presented there.

We next present multiple hierarchical regression analyses. For the US and China results, we present absolute explicit and implicit estimates towards one focal category since these are the groups we would expect to show the greatest ingroup preference (primary sample) and outgroup disdain (origin and political rhetoric fuelling tensions in the US). However, for Italians, British, Black and Brown people, we present the results relative to a reference group (American/White) to create a baseline and to calibrate participants' responses. To create these relative metrics, we subtracted the scores for the largest national and racial categories in the sample (US/White), which were not necessarily every participant's ingroup, from the respective outgroup scores (e.g., Italian, British, Black, and Brown). This exploratory difference-score approach was used because there were no consistent observable effects for British, Italian, Black, and Brown people when using absolute estimates (see SM Appendices X and Y), likely because knowing how a participant rated the reference group was necessary when outgroup prejudice was less uniform. Models predicting the absolute outgroup ratings while adjusting for the reference-group rating are reported in SM Table K5.

The primary hierarchical analyses compared models containing established diseaseavoidance measures, political ideology, individualism, and demographic covariates (Model 1; reported in SM) with models additionally including Ingroup and Outgroup GA (Model 2; Tables 4 5 6 7). We also estimated staged models using the same analytic sample across stages within each outcome. M0 included Outgroup GA alone; M1 added Ingroup GA, general GA, infectability concern, and COVID-19 concern; M2 additionally included political ideology and individualism; and M3 added demographic covariates. We also examined fully adjusted models excluding ideology and individualism in the SM.

We used heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors (MacKinnon & White, 1985), two-sided Wald tests, and 95% confidence intervals. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) was applied across the 16 focal Outgroup GA tests separately within each adjustment stage. Incremental validity was examined through changes in R² when both target-specific indices were added and through the unique contribution of Outgroup GA. Conventional nested-model F-change tests and HC3-based inference were reported separately. Full regression and sensitivity analyses are provided in SM Appendix K.

All additional analyses can be found in the SM or on OSF (https://osf.io/yw3gb/overview?view_only=d9179e8abd084148a65ed918dc5628ed), which also includes the full dataset.

ChatGPT-6 (OpenAI, 2026a) was used to assist with developing R scripts to evaluate the discriminant validity of the four disease-avoidance measures and reproduce the SPSS regression analyses. Additionally, ChatGPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026b) was used to assist with manuscript drafting, improving clarity and organisation, and proofreading. All statistical analyses were executed using SPSS and R, and all AI-assisted content was reviewed by the authors, who retained full responsibility for verifying the results, interpreting the findings, and making final editorial decisions.

Results

Key correlation findings

As expected, Outgroup GA was positively related to Ingroup GA (r(1616) = .65, p < .01) and the original GA subscale (r(1620) = .50, p < .01). Outgroup GA was only weakly related to COVID-19 concern (r(1532) = .07, p < .01) and was unrelated to infectability concerns (r(1619) = .02, p = .534). In contrast, Ingroup GA was positively related to Infectability Concern (r(1617) = .13, p < .001), and more strongly related to COVID-19 concern (r(1529) = .16, p < .001) and the original GA subscale (r(1617) = .65, p < .001). This pattern suggests that the original GA subscale captured more Ingroup than Outgroup GA variance in this dataset. Regarding Political Ideology, the magnitude of the effects reduced going from Outgroup, Ingroup and Original GA (r = .19, .14, and .07, respectively), whereas it was related in the opposite direction to COVID-19 concern (r = -.27) and Infectability Concern (r = -.14), as already demonstrated by O'Shea et al. (2022) using the same dataset.

Overall, the observed correlations between Outgroup GA and the 16 focal outcomes were small (maximum |r| = .19; Appendix G). This argues against simple score redundancy but does not eliminate shared target valence, common-method variance, or measurement error.

[insert Table 2 around here] As shown in Table 2, implicit and matched explicit health/infection scores were positively related for the US (r = .13), China (r = .15), and Italy (r = .11), but not for the UK task (r = -.04). This latter result may reflect the fact that participants explicitly rated British people as only slightly healthier than infected (t(1628) = 2.03, p = .042; M = .07, rescaled from -4 to 4), whereas the other three countries were rated as significantly more infected than healthy (ts < -13.53, ps < .001; American M = -.59; Chinese M = -.59, Italian M = -.60). In contrast, for the BIAT, each group's value was significantly above zero (ts > 2.35, ps <.019), indicating a significant implicit association of that group with healthy rather than infected (scaled from -2 to 2; American M = .22 British M = .11, Italian M = .04), except for China (t(494) = 0.00, p = .997; M = .00), which showed a neutral implicit bias. The overall small effect size relationship between the implicit and explicit scores could be due to (1) measurement error of using reaction time tasks as weak relationship magnitudes are common when using IATs (2) the implicit measures capturing a unique construct, (3) socially desirable responding on the explicit scales due to the sensitive nature of attributing groups of people with infections, or (4) some combination of these factors. However, investigating these possibilities is not the focus of this manuscript.

Discriminant validity of the disease metrics

Confirmatory factor analyses examined the eight matched Ingroup and Outgroup GA items and, separately, all 23 disease-avoidance items (see Table 3). For the eight matched items, a model specifying separate local-context and developing-country-context factors and permitting covariance between residuals for the four matched behavioural scenarios showed the strongest admissible fit (scaled χ²(15) = 108.59, robust CFI = .970, robust RMSEA = .065, SRMR = .047). The factor correlation was .752, 95% CI [.689, .814]. The two-factor model without matched residual covariances was inadmissible because its estimated latent correlation exceeded 1.

Across the broader set of 23 indicators, four-factor models differentiating infectability concern, general germ aversion (GA), ingroup GA, and outgroup GA yielded inadmissible solutions, including the model with matched residual covariances (estimated general GAingroup GA factor correlation = 1.090). A three-factor model combining general and ingroup GA while retaining separate infectability and outgroup GA factors yielded an admissible solution, although global fit remained modest, scaled χ²(223) = 1,589.56, robust CFI = .870, robust RMSEA = .068, SRMR = .059.

[insert Table 3 around here]

These findings indicate that general and ingroup GA were not empirically distinguishable under the models examined, while leaving open the possibility that outgroup GA captures additional context-specific variation. This pattern is substantively relevant: conventional general GA items may predominantly capture aversion in familiar or local contexts and may therefore incompletely represent aversion in outgroup contexts.

Nevertheless, the present analyses do not establish four distinct latent disease-avoidance constructs. We retain the four original composite indices in subsequent tables to preserve the theoretically motivated comparison between general, ingroup, and outgroup germ aversion and to examine their associations with the study outcomes. Their retention allows the overlap between general and ingroup GA to remain visible alongside any differences involving outgroup GA.

Hierarchical Regression Results

Tables 4-7 present the regression results with conventional standard errors and unadjusted significance levels. The hypothesis-support statements below refer to the additional fully adjusted HC3 analyses after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q < .05), reported in Table 8.

Explicit and Implicit preferences towards American and White People (Ingroups) (H1a-H1d)

As shown in Table 4, political ideology was the most consistent predictor of ingroup responses. Greater conservatism was associated with higher US explicit healthy scores, higher US implicit healthy scores, and warmer feelings toward both Americans and White people.

Age, education, religiosity, and Hispanic identity each are related to two of the four ingroup outcomes. COVID-19 concern was related to two outcomes, but in divergent directions: greater concern was associated with rating Americans as less healthy/more infected, while also reporting warmer feelings toward White people. Outgroup GA predicted higher US implicit healthy scores and warmer feelings toward Americans, with a marginal association for warmer feelings toward White people.

Under HC3 inference and multiplicity correction, H1b was supported (American implicit health: β = .103, q = .018). H1c was nominally significant but did not survive correction (American warmth: β = .075, p = .033, q = .052). H1a was not supported, and H1d was directionally consistent but not statistically supported.

[insert Table 4 around here]

Explicit and Implicit Biases against Chinese and Asian People (Outgroups) (H2a-H2d)

Table 5 shows that Outgroup GA and political ideology were the clearest predictors of responses to Chinese and Asian targets. Higher Outgroup GA and greater conservatism were associated with rating Chinese people as less healthy/more infected and with reporting less warmth toward Chinese and Asian people. Outgroup GA also showed a marginal negative association with Chinese implicit health scores. Higher religiosity was associated with greater warmth toward Chinese and Asian people. The remaining predictors showed no consistent pattern.

The HC3 analyses supported H2a, H2c, and H2d after correction: Chinese explicit health (β = -.183, q < .001), Chinese warmth (β = -.157, q < .001), and Asian warmth (β = -.087, q = .030). H2b was directionally consistent but not statistically supported (Chinese implicit health: β = -.124, p = .069, q = .085).

[insert Table 5 around here]

Explicit and Implicit Biases against Italian and Black People (Outgroups) Versus Ingroup (H3a-H3c and H5a)

As shown in Table 6, Outgroup GA was associated with all four Italy/Black outcomes, with the implicit Italy effect marginally significant. Greater Outgroup GA predicted rating Italians as less healthy than Americans, implicitly associating Italians as less healthy than Americans, reporting less warmth toward Italians relative to Americans, and reporting less warmth toward Black people relative to White people. Conservatism was also associated with more negative explicit responses, although it was not related to the implicit Italy score.

As expected, Black participants reported greater preference for Black people and were also more likely to implicitly associate Italians with healthy relative to Americans. The remaining predictors showed no consistent pattern.

With HC3 inference and correction, H3a (Italian-American explicit health), H3c (Italian-American warmth), and H5a (Black-White warmth) were supported (βs = -.097, -.108, and -.098, respectively). H3b, concerning Italian-American implicit health, was directionally consistent but not statistically supported.

[insert Table 6 around here]

Explicit and Implicit Biases against British and Brown People (Outgroups) Versus Ingroup (H4a-H4c and H5b)

As shown in Table 7, outgroup GA and political ideology were again the most consistent predictors. Higher outgroup GA was associated with implicitly rating British people as less healthy than Americans, reporting less warmth toward British people relative to Americans, and reporting less warmth toward Brown people relative to White people. Greater conservatism was associated with rating British people as less healthy than Americans and reporting less warmth toward British and Brown people, but it was unrelated to the implicit British health score. Education, individualism, Black identity, and Hispanic identity each showed two significant effects. The remaining predictors did not show a consistent pattern.

The HC3 analyses supported H4b (British-American implicit health: β = -.245, q = .002) and H5b (Brown-White warmth: β = -.079, q = .044). H4a was not supported; H4c was directionally consistent but not statistically supported after correction.

[insert Table 7 around here]

Robustness and Incremental Validity

Table 8 presents the Outgroup GA coefficients across the four adjustment stages. Of the 16 associations, 12 were significant after correction when unadjusted, 13 after adjustment for the disease-related measures, 12 after adding ideology and individualism, and nine after full adjustment. An otherwise fully adjusted model omitting ideology and individualism yielded 12 corrected associations. Across the fully adjusted models, 14 coefficients had the predicted direction, and 10 were nominally significant.

Adding both target-specific indices to general GA, infectability concern, and COVID-19 concern increased R² by a median of .011 (range: < .001-.038); the conventional incremental F tests remained significant after correction for 13 of 16 outcomes. The unique fully adjusted contribution of Outgroup GA was smaller (median ΔR² = .005), with 10 conventional incremental tests surviving correction. These model-change tests differ from the HC3 coefficient tests, for which nine fully adjusted associations survived correction.

[insert Table 8 around here]

General Discussion

This study examined whether distinguishing Ingroup and Outgroup Germ Aversion (GA) improves the prediction of intergroup attitudes at the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. Across explicit and implicit outcomes, Outgroup GA was associated with ingroup preference and outgroup derogation on several measures, even after controlling for general GA, infectability concern, COVID-19 concern, political ideology, individualism, and demographic covariates. Nine of the 16 fully adjusted associations survived HC3 inference and correction for multiple comparisons, with small increments in explained variance. Ingroup GA, by contrast, contributed little incremental explanatory value. These findings suggest that the target of germ aversion matters: pathogen-avoidance tendencies directed toward foreign or outgroup contexts were more predictive of pandemic-era intergroup attitudes than either general germ aversion or germ aversion directed toward local ingroup contexts. This pattern has both theoretical and applied implications: disease concern may become socially consequential when it is attached to particular groups, places, or ecologies.

Recent meta-analytic evidence further suggests that germ aversion may be more relevant to intergroup attitudes than infectability concern, as general germ aversion shows more consistent associations with outgroup perceptions (Howard et al., 2026). The present study extends that distinction by suggesting that the target of germ aversion may also matter. General GA was associated with some outcomes, but Outgroup GA showed the clearest and most consistent pattern across national and racial targets. The substantial overlap between general GA and Ingroup GA in the broader CFA also raises questions about the contexts represented by conventional germ-aversion measures. Although these findings do not establish that general GA primarily reflects familiar or local contamination concerns, they suggest that the ecological and social contexts embedded within germ-aversion items warrant greater attention when developing and interpreting disease-avoidance measures. This may help explain why broad disease-threat variables, including infectability concern or COVID-19 concern, may sometimes show weak or inconsistent associations with prejudice: they do not capture whether pathogenavoidance concerns are directed toward socially familiar or socially distant targets.

More broadly, the present findings highlight the value of distinguishing the social target of pathogen avoidance. Existing disease-avoidance measures, including general germ-aversion and disgust scales, primarily assess broad concerns about pathogens or contamination without specifying who is perceived as the source of infection (Duncan et al., 2009; Haidt et al., 1994; Tybur et al., 2009). Although measures such as the Intergroup Disgust Sensitivity Scale (Hodson et al., 2013) assess aversive responses toward ethnic outgroups, they do not directly compare matched ingroup and outgroup pathogen concerns using parallel behavioural scenarios. The present adaptation was designed to address this limitation by distinguishing pathogen avoidance directed toward local ingroup contexts from pathogen avoidance directed toward foreign or outgroup contexts. Overall, our findings suggest that specifying the perceived source of contamination may provide a useful conceptual and methodological refinement for applied intergroup research.

At the same time, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence that outgroup membership automatically functions as a pathogen cue. Recent work challenges broad versions of this claim, showing that people are not necessarily more averse to microbe-sharing contact with ethnic outgroup members than ingroup members (Fan et al., 2022), that disease salience did not reliably increase anti-immigrant sentiment during COVID-19 (Fan et al., 2024), and that evidence for broad smoke-detector accounts of pathogen-based prejudice remains mixed (Van Leeuwen et al., 2025). Our findings are more consistent with a conditional account: pathogen-avoidance motives may become socially consequential when outgroup categories are embedded in specific ecological, political, or disease-relevant contexts.

The sociopolitical context of early COVID-19 is therefore central to interpretation. The negative association between outgroup germ aversion and warmth was most pronounced for Chinese and Asian targets, consistent with evidence that anti-Asian prejudice during COVID-19 was shaped by fear, political legitimisation, and racism (Lantz et al., 2023), as well as racialised public discourse connecting COVID-19 to China (Cho et al., 2021; Darling-Hammond et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2023; Reja, 2021). Nevertheless, the pattern was not limited to Chinese or Asian targets. Outgroup GA also predicted less favourable responses toward Italian, British, Black, and Brown targets, suggesting that outgroup-directed pathogen avoidance may generalise beyond the group most explicitly associated with the pandemic's origin, while still varying in strength across targets. This broader pattern suggests that Outgroup GA may index a more general tendency to perceive socially distant groups as potential sources of contamination, rather than concerns uniquely tied to the origins of COVID-19. Such a pattern is consistent with conditional/flexible BIS accounts proposing that pathogen-avoidance motives become socially consequential when groups are perceived as unfamiliar, socially distant, or politically associated with disease risk (Bressan, 2021; Ko et al., 2025; Van Leeuwen et al., 2023).

This broader pattern should be interpreted cautiously: several associations weakened when absolute ratings were adjusted for the comparison-group response, and the racial warmth findings were not statistically supported in the White non-Hispanic subsample. The associations therefore varied with outcome specification and participant subgroup.

Political ideology also played an important role here. Conservatism was a consistent predictor of ingroup preference and outgroup negativity. The staged analyses showed that adding ideology and individualism changed some Outgroup GA associations, indicating shared statistical variance. Such adjustment does not establish that ideology is a mediator, a confounder, or a consequence of Outgroup GA. This caution is especially important given recent evidence that COVID-19 threat did not uniformly increase conservative or exclusionary attitudes (Brandt et al., 2025; Fiagbenu, 2025; Stern & Axt, 2022), and that disease-avoidance responses can flexibly track politicised group cues (Ko et al., 2025). Ideology may therefore be best understood here as a politically meaningful correlate and covariate, but see SM Appendix I for exploratory mediation analyses.

Applied Implications for Health Communication and Intergroup Relations

Public-health communication can have intergroup consequences when a disease threat becomes attached to national, racial, or ethnic categories. This does not mean that health agencies should avoid accurate information about disease emergence, spread, or risk. It does mean that messages linking pathogens to social groups can make those groups salient as contamination sources, especially when political rhetoric already frames them as threatening (Lantz et al., 2023; Ng, 2021; WHO, 2020). Anti-stigma messages should therefore do more than correct misinformation. They should also avoid language that links infectious diseases to particular social groups, nationalities, or ethnic communities, as such messages may encourage people to perceive outgroups as sources of infection. Consistent with World Health Organization guidance, public health communications may benefit from emphasising shared vulnerability, collective responsibility, and people-first language ("people affected by COVID-19" rather than "the infected," "COVID carriers"), while avoiding geographic or ethnic labels that risk reinforcing stigma and social division (WHO, 2020).

The findings also suggest a measurement strategy for applied social psychology.

General disease concerns, perceived infectability, and general GA are useful constructs, but they do not reveal whether pathogen concern is socially targeted. A target-specific measure can help identify when disease avoidance is moving from personal protection to intergroup avoidance. This distinction may be useful for studying social distance, school choice, contact avoidance, immigration attitudes, and trust in public-health guidance during outbreaks.

Related work points in the same direction. Disease salience can interact with attitudes toward foreigners to predict beliefs that avoiding foreigners protects against infection (Krings et al., 2012). COVID-era health-policy contexts can interact with racial avoidance in applied settings such as school choice (Hailey et al., 2023). Disease concerns may also narrow social networks more generally, consistent with evidence that germ aversion predicts smaller friendship networks (Choi & Ackerman, 2026). Taken together, these findings suggest that pathogen-avoidance motives can shape social distance, trust, and intergroup contact, but that these effects depend on social context and target meaning.

Limitations and Future Research

Several limitations qualify the present conclusions. First, the data are cross-sectional and correlational, preventing causal claims about the direction of associations between Outgroup GA and intergroup attitudes. Exploratory indirect-effect analyses (SM Appendix I) suggested that political ideology statistically accounted for part of these associations, with bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero for several outcomes. However, these findings do not establish that political ideology causally mediates the relationship, as all variables were measured concurrently and alternative explanations, including reverse causation and unmeasured confounding, remain plausible. Longitudinal and experimental work is needed to determine whether outgroup-directed pathogen avoidance precedes changes in intergroup attitudes, whether ideology shapes pathogen-avoidance responses, or whether both reflect broader social and political orientations.

Second, the adapted Ingroup and Outgroup GA measures showed low internal consistency using conventional coefficient alpha. These scales were intentionally constructed from four matched behavioural scenarios (e.g., toilets, street food, hand sanitiser, and water bottles) rather than multiple interchangeable indicators of a single behaviour. Supplementary psychometric analyses suggested that responses reflected both context-related germ aversion and systematic variance associated with the behavioural scenario itself. An eight-item correlated-uniqueness confirmatory factor model, which allowed matched Ingroup and Outgroup GA items to share residual variance, provided an admissible solution with acceptable fit, whereas the conventional two-factor model was inadmissible. However, the broader CFA examining all four disease-avoidance measures did not establish four distinct latent constructs: the four-factor model was inadmissible, and the alternative three-factor model showed limited overall fit. These findings provide preliminary evidence of context-related variance after accounting for matched scenarios, but they do not eliminate measurement error or establish complete discriminant validity among the disease-avoidance measures or between these measures and intergroup attitudes. The adapted measures should therefore be treated as provisional indices rather than fully validated scales. Further refinement and validation using larger item pools and independent samples are needed.

Third, the Outgroup GA items may conflate several theoretically distinct cues.

References to developing or foreign countries may capture outgroup status, foreign ecology, socioeconomic stereotypes (e.g., Sng et al., 2025), perceived hygiene norms, and pathogen concerns simultaneously. This ambiguity is not merely a measurement nuisance; it may reflect how people actually infer disease risk from social and ecological cues. However, future research should experimentally separate these elements by comparing wording based on foreignness, ecological unfamiliarity, pathogen prevalence, socioeconomic development, and specific national or racial targets.

Fourth, the sample consisted of self-selected Project Implicit volunteers rather than a nationally representative sample. Although Project Implicit samples often show patterns comparable to broader survey data on many implicit and explicit attitudes (Charlesworth & Banaji, 2019; Freichel & O'Shea, 2023), replication in representative and non-WEIRD samples is needed (Henrich et al., 2010). Cross-cultural tests are especially important because relationships among pathogen avoidance, ideology, and prejudice may differ across political systems, histories of intergroup contact, and local disease ecologies.

Finally, the study was conducted during the early phase of COVID-19, when uncertainty, political rhetoric, and disease salience were unusually high. This timing is a strength because it captures intergroup attitudes during a naturally occurring health crisis, but it may also limit generalisability to non-pandemic contexts. Future studies should test whether Outgroup GA predicts intergroup attitudes during periods of lower disease salience and whether the same patterns emerge when disease threat is experimentally manipulated.

Conclusion

This study provides preliminary evidence that outgroup-directed germ aversion is a useful predictor of intergroup attitudes during a pandemic. Outgroup GA was more consistently associated with ingroup preference and outgroup derogation than Ingroup GA, general GA, infectability concern, or COVID-19 concern. These findings support a target-specific approach to pathogen-avoidance psychology. For applied social psychology, the central point is that disease-avoidance motives may be most informative for intergroup relations when researchers specify who or what is perceived as the source of contamination. At the same time, the results support a cautious, conditional account rather than a broad claim that outgroups are automatically treated as pathogen threats. Further psychometric refinement and experimental validation are needed before the adapted Ingroup and Outgroup GA scales can be recommended for widespread use. More broadly, the present findings suggest that identifying who is perceived as the source of contamination may be important for understanding when disease-avoidance processes translate into intergroup conflict and demonstrate why this targetspecific distinction warrants further theoretical and psychometric development.

Evolutionary Human Sciences, 6, e34. https://doi.org/10.1017/ehs.2024.28 Core component Operationalisation in this study Why it is not identical to the other constructs Infectability concern Belief about personal susceptibility to illness Seven PVD self-report items; 1-7 agreement scale Concerns the respondent's vulnerability, not avoidance behaviour or evaluation of a social group. General germ aversion (GA) Behavioural discomfort in possible pathogen-transmission situations Eight PVD self-report items with no specified social source Specifies avoidance behaviour but not whether the potential source is local, foreign, or a named group. Ingroup GA Avoidance of the same contamination scenarios located in the respondent's local region Four matched scenarios: public toilets, street food, hand sanitiser, water-bottle sharing Self-reported behavioural tolerance across local contexts; does not ask whether Americans or White people (primary sample) are healthy or liked. Outgroup GA Avoidance of the same contamination scenarios in foreign/developing-country contexts Four matched scenarios referring to developing or foreign countries Self-reported behavioural tolerance across contexts; does not evaluate any named national or racial target. Wording may nevertheless cue foreignness, development, hygiene, or ecology stereotypes. Explicit health/infectious ness judgement Perceived association of a named group with healthy versus infected Single item for American, Chinese, Italian, and British people A direct judgement about a named group's health status rather than the respondent's own avoidance behaviour. Feeling thermometer Global affective evaluation of a named group Single 0 (cold) -10 (warm) item for national and racial targets Captures broad liking/warmth, which can arise from contact, identity, ideology, stereotypes, and many non-pathogen processes. BIAT health association Response-time (RT) association between a social category and healthy versus infected attributes Absolute RT DD scores and relative D scores. Task-based category-attribute association; not a selfreport scale and not a direct measure of behavioural germ avoidance. Note. PVD = Perceived Vulnerability to Disease; BIAT = Brief Implicit Association Test; DD = decomposed D-score. The distinctions describe conceptual and operational differences and do not, by themselves, establish discriminant validity. Note. = ∓ p <.10, *= p <.05, ** = p <.01, *** = p < .001. Appendix H Pre-analysis Checks and Details About Outliers Pre-analysis Checks

There was no evidence of multicollinearity in the predictor variables for any of the analyses (explicit and implicit) in the bivariate correlations, using the Pearson Correlation coefficient with rs < 0.9. There was no evidence of singularity; all tolerances > 0.1, and all VIF values were < 10. Substantial outliers (> 3 S.D) were removed, and all maximal cooks' distances were within limits. Furthermore, residual errors were normally distributed, and homoscedastic (see below for more details). Skewness and kurtosis values were within limits for all variables, except for the comparative race variables (e.g., Asian or Not Asian). The skewness values for the race categories were as follows: Asian: 2.358, Black: 3.031, Hispanic: 2.299, Other: 2.87.

Despite the high skewness values for these variables, the decision was made not to transform the data. This choice was made to accurately reflect the population characteristics being studied but also skewness would be expected due to the imbalance in sample size relative to the more common contrast category (White) found in this dataset.

These counts describe exploratory associations and do not provide a comparison of causal models.

Limits on Interpretation

All variables were measured in the same study session. The analyses therefore cannot establish that Outgroup GA preceded political ideology or that ideology preceded intergroup attitudes. The terms direct and indirect in the reproduced diagrams refer to coefficients in the specified statistical models, not established causal effects. We do not interpret "full" or "partial mediation" classifications as evidence that a psychological process has been identified.

Reverse and reciprocal associations are plausible. Existing negative outgroup attitudes could increase discomfort with outgroup-linked contamination scenarios. Political ideology, broader negative perceptions of unfamiliar groups, or other unmeasured factors could contribute to both responses. Covariate adjustment does not rule out these explanations or establish that all relevant confounding has been addressed.

Reversing the predictor and intermediate variable does not resolve the temporal-ordering problem. The fact that one ordering produced more nominally significant indirect effects cannot establish that it is the correct causal ordering. Similarly, bootstrap intervals quantify sampling uncertainty under the fitted model; they do not test its causal assumptions.

The adapted germ-aversion measures have modest internal consistency, and the developing-country wording may combine pathogen concern, foreignness, socioeconomic stereotypes, and negative group evaluation. Measurement error and construct overlap may affect the path estimates. The composites also combine distinct targets and, in some cases, explicit and implicit outcomes; a composite association does not establish an identical association for each component.

These analyses were exploratory and were not preregistered. The 95% bootstrap intervals were not adjusted for the number of models and outcomes examined. They should therefore be interpreted as nominal, hypothesis-generating intervals and should not be equated with the multiplicity-adjusted regression results in Appendix K.

The self-selected U.S. sample and early-pandemic context limit generalisation. These analyses do not show that changing political ideology would alter the Outgroup GA-attitude association, or that reducing germ aversion would reduce prejudice. They remain outside the main evidential argument. Exploratory Indirect Associations: American/White and Chinese/Asian Absolute Composite Outcomes Note. Internal consistency

Internal-consistency estimates were modest for the adapted Ingroup GA (α = .47) and Outgroup GA (α = .55) measures, based on four items each (Table Z1). The corresponding mean inter-item correlations were .17 and .24. Across the two original PVD subscales, the cleanedsample alpha estimates were .89 for infectability concern and .71 for general GA. The reliability estimates vary by itemwise complete-case sample size.

Item analyses

Corrected item-total correlations ranged from .21 to .55 for the ingroup scale and from .35 to .52 for the outgroup scale (Table Z2). The public toilet and hand sanitiser items demonstrated the strongest associations with their respective total scores, whereas the water bottle items showed comparatively weaker item-total correlations in both scales.

Item deletion analyses indicated that removal of any individual item produced little improvement in internal consistency. Although deleting the water bottle items produced the largest increase in coefficient alpha, reliability remained modest, suggesting that no single item fully accounted for the modest internal consistency, although behavioural heterogeneity may have contributed. Consequently, all four items were retained to preserve conceptual coverage of the adapted construct.

Item response theory analyses

To provide an estimate of item functioning and measurement precision, graded response models were estimated separately for the ingroup and outgroup GA scales. Item discrimination parameters varied across behavioural scenarios. For the ingroup GA scale, the public toilet item showed the strongest discrimination, whereas the water bottle item showed weak discrimination. For the outgroup GA scale, discrimination parameters were more evenly distributed, although the water bottle item again showed comparatively weaker performance. Marginal reliability estimates were .69 for the ingroup GA scale and .64 for the outgroup GA scale. These values provide complementary estimates of model-based measurement precision, although they do not negate the modest coefficient alpha values.

However, given the small number of items and the heterogeneous behavioural scenarios sampled, the IRT results should be interpreted as supplementary descriptive evidence rather than definitive validation of the scales.

Overall interpretation

The brief adapted scales show modest internal consistency, and the ingroup items are especially heterogeneous. PCA and item-level analyses provide descriptive information about the scoring of each index, but they do not establish discriminant validity. The admissible eight-item two-factor correlated-uniqueness model suggests that the local-context and developing-country-context responses can be differentiated under the fitted model after accounting for substantial shared behavioural-scenario variance; its latent factor correlation of .752 nonetheless indicates overlap. The broader 23-item results provide a more stringent qualification: a four-factor solution was inadmissible, and the admissible merged three-factor solution had limited global fit. These indices are therefore best treated as provisional contextspecific measures in the present study. They do not isolate membership of social groups from differences in ecological familiarity, hygiene beliefs, or perceived socioeconomic development. Independent replication and item development are needed.

Rationale

The ingroup and outgroup germ aversion (GA) measures used in the present study were adapted from the Germ Aversion subscale of the Perceived Vulnerability to Disease (PVD) scale (Duncan et al., 2009). Whereas the original PVD assesses perceived infectability and general germ aversion, the present adaptation was designed to compare contamination responses framed in participants' local regions (Ingroup GA) and in developing-country contexts (Outgroup GA).

To maintain direct comparability between the two measures, each ingroup item was paired with an equivalent outgroup item describing the same behavioural scenario (e.g., avoiding public toilets, eating street food, using hand sanitiser, and sharing a water bottle), using the same behavioural content but different contextual wording ("my local region" versus "developing countries").

The primary aim of these measures was to provide an initial test of the theoretical distinction between ingroup and outgroup germ aversion rather than to develop a comprehensive psychometric instrument. Consequently, each scale consisted of only four items sampling distinct pathogen-avoidance behaviours. Such brief scales often produce modest estimates of coefficient alpha because they contain relatively few items (Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994; Streiner, 2003) and intentionally assess heterogeneous behavioural contexts rather than multiple interchangeable indicators of a single behaviour. Coefficient alpha alone does not establish whether these indices are unidimensional or adequately reliable; the low values nevertheless represent a substantive measurement limitation.

Accordingly, we conducted a series of supplementary psychometric analyses to better characterise the measurement properties of the adapted scales. These analyses were not intended to establish definitive validation of the measures, but rather to characterise item associations, potential sources of shared variance, and measurement limitations arising from the scale design.

The correlated-uniqueness model was considered particularly important because each ingroup item was intentionally paired with an equivalent outgroup item describing the identical behavioural scenario. Consequently, responses were expected to reflect not only target-specific germ aversion (ingroup vs. outgroup), but also shared variance attributable to the behavioural context itself (e.g., public toilets, street food, hand sanitiser, or water bottles). Ignoring shared variance between paired behavioural scenarios can impair the fit of simple latent-factor models and distort estimated correlations between factors. However, accounting for these cross-scale residual covariances does not, by itself, establish adequate within-scale reliability.

Taken together, these analyses provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the adapted measures than coefficient alpha alone and allow a more nuanced interpretation of their psychometric properties. Rather than relying exclusively on a single reliability coefficient, the analyses evaluate multiple complementary sources of evidence regarding the internal structure, measurement precision, and construct representation of the adapted ingroup and outgroup germ aversion measures.

We evaluated internal consistency, principal component structure, corrected item-total associations, item-deletion diagnostics, confirmatory measurement models, and graded-response item response theory (IRT) models. The CFA comparisons included one-and two-factor representations of the eight matched context-specific items and alternative structures for all 23

Exploratory principal component analyses

To provide an additional descriptive assessment of internal structure, separate principal component analyses (PCAs) were conducted for the four ingroup GA items and the four outgroup GA items. These analyses were exploratory and should be interpreted alongside the broader reliability, item-level, and confirmatory factor analyses reported here.

For the ingroup GA scale, the PCA yielded a one-component solution with an eigenvalue of 1.55, explaining 38.7% of the variance. Item loadings ranged from .383 to .774. The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin value was marginal, KMO = .568, whereas Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant, χ²(6) = 356.37, p < .001. The reverse-scored item "I am comfortable sharing a water bottle with a stranger from my local region" showed the weakest loading, λ = .383, and the lowest communality, h² = .15, suggesting weaker alignment with the overall ingroup GA component than the other items.

For the outgroup GA scale, the PCA also yielded a one-component solution, with an eigenvalue of 1.73, explaining 43.3% of the variance. Item loadings ranged from .546 to .723, and communalities ranged from .30 to .52. The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin value was higher than for the ingroup GA scale, KMO = .638, and Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant, χ²(6) = 527.48, p < .001. These results indicate that the outgroup GA items showed a clearer onecomponent structure than the ingroup GA items.

Taken together, the PCA results provide preliminary descriptive support for scoring each adapted GA measure as a brief unidimensional index, while also indicating that the ingroup GA scale had weaker internal structure than the outgroup GA scale. Confirmatory factor analyses of the eight matched items

The four ingroup and four outgroup items were analysed using one-and two-factor models, with and without residual covariances for matched scenarios. The two-factor model without matched residuals was inadmissible (estimated factor correlation = 1.227). The admissible two-factor correlated-uniqueness model showed robust CFI = .970, robust RMSEA = .065, and SRMR = .047, compared with robust CFI = .934, robust RMSEA = .094, and SRMR = .051 for the admissible one-factor correlated-uniqueness model (Table Z3). The correlation between the local-context and developing-country-context factors was .752, 95% CI [.689, .814].

Because the one-factor model corresponds to a boundary constraint on the two-factor latent correlation, the models are compared descriptively using fit indices and likelihood-based BIC rather than relying on a conventional chi-square difference reference test. These findings provide evidence of partial target-context differentiation once shared behavioural scenarios are modelled, not definitive construct validation.

Confirmatory factor analyses of all 23 disease-avoidance items

The 23-item CFA compared models separating perceived infectability from germ aversion and differentiating general, local-context, and developing-country-context GA. The four-factor models, both with and without matched residual covariances, were inadmissible. In the four-factor correlated-uniqueness model, the estimated general GA-Ingroup GA factor correlation was 1.090. The alternative model combining general and local-context GA into a single factor, with separate infectability and developing-country-context GA factors, yielded an admissible solution and the lowest BIC among the models with paired residual covariances (Table Z4). However, this model did not achieve strong overall fit (scaled χ²(223) = 1,589.56, robust CFI = .870, robust RMSEA = .068, SRMR = .059). Accordingly, the results do not establish four discriminable latent factors. They suggest substantial overlap between general and local-context GA, with some differentiation of developing-country-context responses that requires independent validation.

All regression coefficients are standardised (β). The same analytic sample was used across adjustment stages within each outcome. M0 = Outgroup GA alone; M1 = M0 plus Ingroup GA, general GA, infectability concern, and COVID-19 concern; M2 = M1 plus political ideology and individualism; M3 = M2 plus age, gender, socioeconomic status, education, religiosity, and race/ethnicity indicators. Boldface in the M0-M3 β columns and the M3 p column indicates an unadjusted, two-sided HC3 normal-reference p < .05; boldface in the M3 q column indicates Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted q < .05 across the 16 focal Outgroup GA tests. Confidence intervals for M3 also use HC3 standard errors and normal-reference critical values. Support classifications are based on M3: Supported = predicted direction with q < .05; Nominal only = predicted direction with p < .05 but q ≥ .05; Direction only = predicted direction with p ≥ .05; Not supported = no evidence meeting these criteria. Bold coefficients based on nominal p values do not necessarily survive multiple-testing correction.

Confirmatory factor analysis model comparisonsAll models were estimated with MLR. Matched residuals allow covariance between the ingroup and outgroup versions of each behavioural scenario. Inadmissible indicates estimated factor correlations outside the range -1 to 1. CFI and RMSEA are robust indices; TLI is the scaled index. χ² values are scaled; BIC is based on the unscaled log-likelihood, not χ²-scaled plus a penalty. The reported χ² values are model-fit statistics, not χ² difference tests.Four-factor models specified infectability concern, general GA, Ingroup GA, and Outgroup GA. The merged model combines general and local-context GA. The fourfactor models returned inadmissible factor correlations; thus, model-fit indices alone do not validate these solutions. BIC is likelihood-based and is compared only within the same item set and sample. Robust CFI, scaled TLI, robust RMSEA, and SRMR are reported.
